evidence.claim: A mountain road climbs through cliffs, aspens and lava toward Panguitch.
evidence.quote: Heading east, the road descends through a thick aspen forest

evidence.claim: A mountain road climbs through cliffs, aspens and lava toward Panguitch.
evidence.quote: Ancient lava fields pop up through the aspen trees that line the highway.

evidence.claim: Utah’s Patchwork Parkway climbs from Parowan through red and white cliffs, then crosses high country before descending through aspens and lava fields to Panguitch.
evidence.quote: From Parowan, the highway climbs past the colorful Vermilion Cliffs through a maple and scrub oak forest. The road twists through cone-shaped white cliffs then makes a major ascent to the forested heights of Brian Head ski town.

evidence.claim: Utah’s Patchwork Parkway climbs from Parowan through red and white cliffs, then crosses high country before descending through aspens and lava fields to Panguitch.
evidence.quote: Heading east, the road descends through a thick aspen forest

evidence.claim: Visit Utah gives the drive as 50 miles and 1.5 hours, highlighting the changing cliffs, forests, meadows and lakes along SR 143.
evidence.quote: Time: 1.5 hours Distance: 50 miles

evidence.claim: highlighting the changing cliffs, forests, meadows and lakes along SR 143.
evidence.quote: Every bend in the road brings into vision a new patch of scenery from colorful rocky cliffs and spires, alpine forests, lush meadows with rambling streams, crystal blue lakes

evidence.claim: It became a National Scenic Byway in 2009.
evidence.quote: (8) Utah's Patchwork Parkway National Scenic Byway. (a) Comprised of Brian Head-Panguitch Lake State Scenic Byway. (b) Designated National Scenic Byway October 16, 2009.

evidence.claim: The western road began as a wagon route built by Mormon settlers to reach timber above Parowan.
evidence.quote: The town of Parowan was settled in 1851 by Mormon pioneers, who built a wagon road up Parowan Canyon to access timber for buildings.

evidence.claim: S. A. Halterman drove an automobile to Cedar Breaks through the canyon in 1919; improvements allowed him to take visitors weekly by 1921.
evidence.quote: In 1919, S. A. Halterman took the first automobile to Cedar Breaks via Parowan Canyon. With improvements to the road completed by 1921, he was able to take visitors on weekly trips to the area.

evidence.claim: SR 143 was commissioned in 1933, and its extension to Panguitch came in 1985.
evidence.quote: State Route 143 was first commissioned in 1933 as the road from Parowan to the Dixie National Forest boundary.

evidence.claim: its extension to Panguitch came in 1985.
evidence.quote: again in 1985 to its present-day eastern end in Panguitch.

evidence.claim: The initial state route stopped at the Dixie National Forest boundary. A 1953 extension took the designation to Cedar Breaks’ north boundary, before the later addition of Panguitch Lake Road.
evidence.quote: The route was extended in 1953 to reach from U.S. Route 91 (former State Route 1) in Parowan (Main Street) to the north boundary of Cedar Breaks National Monument

evidence.claim: The Patchwork name recalls an earlier mountain crossing for food.
evidence.quote: Early settlers desperate for food once crossed the plateau in midwinter using handmade quilts laid atop deep snow to reach settlements to the west.

evidence.claim: After frost killed most of Panguitch’s first settlers’ crops, seven men set out for supplies. They reportedly laid quilts on the snow to keep from sinking after abandoning their wagons.
evidence.quote: At a crisis point, seven men left the community to seek flour and foodstuffs from surrounding communities. Heavy snow forced the abandonment of wagons and teams, and the men had no option but to continue on foot, reportedly by laying one quilt after another upon the snow to keep from sinking in too deeply.

evidence.claim: After frost killed most of Panguitch’s first settlers’ crops
evidence.quote: most of the settlers' initial crops were killed by frost before they could mature.

evidence.claim: From Parowan, climb past Brian Head to Cedar Breaks’ North View.
evidence.quote: The byway continues south past the North View of Cedar Breaks where it junctions with SR-148.

evidence.claim: Turn east through the aspen and lava country to Panguitch Lake, then follow pastures and Panguitch Creek into Panguitch.
evidence.quote: The byway continues east, following lush pastures and the banks of the Panguitch Creek into historic Panguitch town.

evidence.claim: Turn east through the aspen and lava country to Panguitch Lake
evidence.quote: The road meets up with Panguitch Lake which is popular for fishing and boating.

evidence.claim: At Cedar Breaks, erosion has cut a natural amphitheater three miles across and more than 2,000 feet deep.
evidence.quote: Cedar Breaks is a natural amphitheater, stretching across 3 miles (4.8 km), with a depth of over 2,000 feet (610 m).

evidence.claim: SR 143 passes its North View before meeting SR 148.
evidence.quote: The byway continues south past the North View of Cedar Breaks where it junctions with SR-148.

evidence.claim: The canyon’s shale, limestone and sandstone began as deposits in ancient Lake Claron. Uplift raised those layers, and erosion wore them away over millions of years.
evidence.quote: Uplift and erosion formed the canyon over millions of years, raising and then wearing away the shale, limestone, and sandstone that were deposited at the bottom of an ancient lake

evidence.claim: Iron oxides give the rock reds, oranges and yellows; manganese oxides contribute purple.
evidence.quote: Iron oxides provide the reds, oranges and yellows, while manganese oxides provide shades of purple.

evidence.claim: Above the canyon, bristlecone pines grow in the high country, including specimens more than 1,600 years old.
evidence.quote: The bristlecone pine, a species of tree that is known as the longest living single organism, can also be found in the high country, with some local specimens known to be more than 1600 years old.

evidence.claim: Subalpine meadows also dot the rim, including the Alpine Pond area.
evidence.quote: Subalpine meadows dot the canyon rim in such areas as Alpine Pond

evidence.claim: Look for red, orange and yellow rock colored by iron oxides, with purple from manganese oxides.
evidence.quote: Iron oxides provide the reds, oranges and yellows, while manganese oxides provide shades of purple.

evidence.claim: SR 148 generally closes from mid-November through late May. SR 143 between Brian Head and Panguitch is subject to bad-weather closures.
evidence.quote: The road generally closes from mid-November through late May to become a groomed trail for snowmobiles, x-country skiing, and snowshoeing.

evidence.claim: SR 148 generally closes from mid-November through late May. SR 143 between Brian Head and Panguitch is subject to bad-weather closures.
evidence.quote: The portion between Brian Head and Panguitch is subject to closure in bad weather.

evidence.claim: The Parowan–Brian Head approach has grades reaching 13 percent and is not recommended for RVs or semi-trucks.
evidence.quote: The grade reaches 13% in some places, precipitous enough that travel by RVs or semi trucks is not recommended.

evidence.claim: Panguitch Lake was a natural lake before a 24-foot dam enlarged it into a reservoir.
evidence.quote: Panguitch Lake () was originally a large natural lake (777 acres) that has now been expanded by the creation of a 24-foot (7 m) dam

evidence.claim: The original water covered 777 acres; the reservoir’s maximum surface area is 1,248 acres.
evidence.quote: to become a reservoir with a maximum surface area of 1,248 acres (5 km2).

evidence.claim: The original water covered 777 acres
evidence.quote: was originally a large natural lake (777 acres)

evidence.claim: It lies on the Markagunt Plateau between Cedar Breaks and Panguitch and drains into the Sevier River.
evidence.quote: The lake, which drains into the Sevier River is located on the Markagunt Plateau, between Panguitch, Utah and Cedar Breaks National Monument.

evidence.claim: The lake’s earliest known use was as a Paiute fishery, and its name means “big fish” in the Paiute language.
evidence.quote: The earliest known use of Panguitch Lake was as a fishery by Paiute Indians (Panguitch means "big fish" in the Paiute language).

evidence.claim: SR 143 supplies road access to the lake, which the local tourism bureau identifies with fishing and boating.
evidence.quote: The road meets up with Panguitch Lake which is popular for fishing and boating.

evidence.claim: SR 143 supplies road access to the lake
evidence.quote: Road access to the lake is provided by Utah State Route 143

evidence.claim: The lake lies within Dixie National Forest.
evidence.quote: The lake is located in the Dixie National Forest

evidence.claim: Rose-colored brick houses in Panguitch carry the story of wages paid in building material.
evidence.quote: Workers were paid in bricks, which they used to build their own houses. Rose-colored brick houses still stand in Panguitch.

evidence.claim: Settlers fired local clay in kilns; workers used their brick pay to build homes.
evidence.quote: The settlers used kilns to process local clay into rose-colored bricks. Workers were paid in bricks, which they used to build their own houses.

evidence.claim: The historic district’s houses also reveal a local building pattern: many have square plans, pyramidal roofs and projecting bays.
evidence.quote: Many houses are of a distinctive local style with a square plan and a pyramidal roof, incorporating projecting bays.

evidence.claim: Most district residences date from 1890 to 1930. Many buildings use deep-red, soft-edged brick produced near Panguitch between 1915 and 1940, adding another chapter to the town’s use of local clay.
evidence.quote: Most of the buildings in the district are residences built between 1890 and 1930, with a proportion of commercial buildings at the center of town. Most buildings are built in red brick, many using a distinctive deep red brick with soft edges that was produced near Panguitch between 1915 and 1940.

evidence.claim: At the Ira Hatch House, a square tower combines with a mix of Victorian Eclectic and Queen Anne details.
evidence.quote: with a mix of Victorian Eclectic and Queen Anne elements such as the square tower

evidence.claim: At the Ira Hatch House, a square tower combines with a mix of Victorian Eclectic and Queen Anne details.
evidence.quote: The most prominent and substantial house is the Ira Hatch House (1896)

evidence.claim: Look for brick houses with square plans, pyramidal roofs and projecting bays.
evidence.quote: Many houses are of a distinctive local style with a square plan and a pyramidal roof, incorporating projecting bays.
